summary: KV-cache-quant fallback to F16 after a failed q8_0 context init keeps the n_ctx that was sized assuming the smaller q8_0 footprint, roughly doubling actual KV-cache memory on exactly the memory-tight devices this sizing exists to protect.
failure_scenario: KVCachePolicy.recommend() picks Q8_0 only when headroom < 1.2GB (e.g. appBudgetGb=1.8, modelWeightsGb=0.9 -> headroom=0.765GB). ContextWindow.recommend(appBudgetGb, modelWeightsGb, Q8_0) then scales n_ctx by /0.53 (~1.9x) versus the F16-safe value: base=2048 for that headroom bracket, scaled/rounded to n_ctx=3840. nativeLoad (llama_jni.cpp:412-415) sets cp.type_k/type_v = GGML_TYPE_Q8_0 and calls llama_init_from_model with cp.n_ctx=3840. If that context init fails because the model/backend lacks flash-attention support for a quantized V-cache (a real llama.cpp constraint, explicitly anticipated by the comment at line 408-411 and the retry at 417-425), the code retries with F16 KV cache at the SAME cp.n_ctx=3840 (line 422-424) instead of recomputing n_ctx for F16 (which would have been 2048 for that headroom). F16 costs ~1.9x more memory per token than Q8_0, so the actual KV-cache allocation ends up sized for a much larger memory budget than the device has -- risking a native-heap OOM / low-memory-kill mid-conversation on precisely the constrained phones that were routed to Q8_0 in the first place.
suggested_fix: On the q8_0->f16 fallback, either recompute a safe n_ctx for F16 (e.g. reuse ContextWindow.recommend(appBudgetGb, modelWeightsGb, KVCacheType.F16) on the Kotlin side and pass it down, or shrink cp.n_ctx by the KVCacheType.Q8_0.relativeCostPerToken ratio before retrying) so the fallback context never exceeds the memory budget the original sizing assumed.

verdict.reason: Confirmed by reading llama_jni.cpp:394-426. cp.n_ctx is set once from the Kotlin-computed context_tokens (sized assuming q8_0's 0.53x per-token cost) and is never recomputed on the F16 fallback retry at lines 421-424 -- only type_k/type_v change back to F16. Cross-checked KVCachePolicy.kt and ContextWindow.kt: the 3-arg ContextWindow.recommend() scales base n_ctx by 1/relativeCostPerToken, so a q8_0-sized n_ctx (e.g. 3840 for the cited headroom bracket) is genuinely ~1.9x an F16-safe n_ctx (2048) for the same headroom. The comment block at lines 408-411/418-420 explicitly documents this fallback as an anticipated real scenario (models whose FLASH_ATTN_TYPE_AUTO resolves to disabled), so this is not a hypothetical or dead path -- it's a real, reachable, unmitigated memory-sizing bug on exactly the memory-tight devices the whole KV-quant system exists to protect.

summary: A resumed download's HTTP 206 response is trusted without verifying that the server's Content-Range actually starts at the requested offset, so a misbehaving/non-compliant server can silently misalign appended bytes.
failure_scenario: JvmHttpRangeClient.open() sends `Range: bytes=$offsetBytes-` and treats any 206 (HTTP_PARTIAL) response as `resumed = true` (line 46), then totalBytes() (line 66-77) only parses the total size out of Content-Range, never the range START, before the caller (ModelDownloadEngine.download) appends the new body directly onto the existing `.part` file via JvmFileSink.append (seek to end, write). If a CDN/proxy returns 206 but actually serves the resource from byte 0 (ignoring the Range header while still using status 206 instead of 200), the appended bytes are the wrong slice and the resulting `.part` file is corrupted at the byte range where the two segments meet. The project's own docs/BUG_JOURNAL.md documents this exact pattern ("H9: verify a 206's Content-Range start before appending") as already fixed on the TS/desktop twin, but the Android JVM implementation was never given the same check.
suggested_fix: Parse the `start` value out of the Content-Range header (`bytes start-end/total`) and compare it to `offsetBytes`; if it doesn't match (or the header is missing on a 206), treat the response like a non-resumable 200: truncate the `.part` file and restart from 0, exactly as the existing 200-with-partial-existing branch (ModelDownloadEngine.kt:136-139) already does.

verdict.reason: Confirmed by reading JvmDownloadIO.kt. open() at line 46 sets resumed=true from HTTP 206 alone, and totalBytes() (66-77) only extracts the size after the '/' in Content-Range, never validating the range START against the requested offsetBytes, before ModelDownloadEngine.download appends new bytes onto the existing .part via JvmFileSink.append (seek-to-end, write). No code anywhere in this file cross-checks a Content-Range start. The project's own docs/BUG_JOURNAL.md (line 274, H9) documents exactly this class of bug -- 'verify a 206's Content-Range start before appending' -- as a lesson already applied elsewhere (TS/desktop twin), confirming this is a real, previously-identified pattern that the Android JVM implementation genuinely lacks. Requires a non-RFC-compliant server/proxy to trigger, which is a real (if not universal) class of misbehavior for CDNs/proxies, so this is a legitimate defensive gap, not a fabricated scenario.

summary: The failed-model-switch restore path only reloads the previous model when its id differs from the one that just failed to load, so re-loading (retrying) the currently-active model and having that retry fail leaves the engine with no model loaded and no restore attempted.
failure_scenario: acceptAndPrepare(model) captures `previousId = engine.loadedModelId` (line 192) before calling engine.load(model, path). LlamaEngine.load() unconditionally frees the currently-loaded native handle BEFORE attempting to load the new one (LlamaEngine.kt:131), so the engine is left with handle==0 the instant the old model is freed. If `engine.load()` then throws (line 210) while `model.id == previousId` (e.g. the user retries loading the model that is already active, or a picker re-selects the current model and the reload transiently fails -- OOM blip, corrupted-then-re-verified file, thermal condition), the restore logic at line 214-216 computes `previous = previousId?.takeIf { it != model.id }` which evaluates to null specifically because model.id == previousId, so `restore(previous)` is never attempted and the code falls straight to `phase = OnboardingPhase.Failed(...)` at line 221 -- even though the previously-working model's file is still on disk and reloadable. The user is left with the engine completely unloaded (no model, chat unusable) despite a working model being one `engine.load()` call away, unlike the genuine cross-model switch case which is correctly protected.
suggested_fix: Don't special-case `previousId == model.id` out of the restore path -- attempt `restore` using `previousId` regardless of whether it equals the model that just failed, since LlamaEngine.load() always frees the old handle first; the restore call will simply reload the same file again, which is safe and idempotent.

verdict.reason: The cited code (OnboardingModel.kt:192-221) does behave as described in isolation, but the failure scenario is not reachable through any real call site. Traced every production caller of acceptAndPrepare(model) in android/app: MainTabs' onSelectModel is only wired from ModelPickerSheet, whose row is explicitly disabled for the currently-active model (`val enabled = fitness.canLoad && !isCurrent`, ModelPickerSheet.kt:140) AND both call sites additionally guard with `if (picked.id != model.id) onSelectModel(picked)` (ChatScreen.kt:563, SettingsScreen.kt:381), and SettingsScreen's quick-preset buttons carry the same `id != model.id` guard (lines 120/123/126). The only other caller, restoreAtLaunch()/onAccept() in the first-run onboarding path, only fires while phase==Idle/Recommended, before any model has ever been loaded (engine.loadedModelId is null at that point), so previousId is null and the described 'model.id == previousId' collision can't occur there either. Every real UI path structurally prevents model.id from ever equaling the already-loaded model's id when acceptAndPrepare is invoked, so this fails the reachability lens.

summary: load() frees the old native handle and clears loadedModelId but does not clear loadedContextTokens, so a failed reload leaves loadedContextTokens holding a stale non-null value from the freed model even though the documented contract says it is null whenever nothing is loaded.
failure_scenario: LlamaEngine.load(): line 131 frees the previous handle and sets `handle = 0L; loadedModelId = null` but leaves `loadedContextTokens` untouched. If the subsequent `nativeLoad(...)` call fails (returns 0, line 144-145 throws IllegalStateException), the engine is left with handle==0 and loadedModelId==null (i.e. "nothing loaded" per ensureReady()'s own check at line 220) while `loadedContextTokens` still reports the PREVIOUS model's real n_ctx (e.g. 2048) instead of null. Any caller that reads `engine.loadedContextTokens` directly to decide context-window sizing (ChatModel.kt:194) without first checking readiness gets a stale, non-representative window size for a model that is no longer loaded -- inconsistent with the class doc comment at LlamaEngine.kt:38-41 ("or null when nothing is loaded").
suggested_fix: Set `loadedContextTokens = null` alongside `handle = 0L; loadedModelId = null` at the top of load() (line 131), the same reset unload() already performs, so the field never holds a stale value while the engine reports 'nothing loaded'.

verdict.reason: The code fact is accurate -- LlamaEngine.load() (line 131) clears handle/loadedModelId but not loadedContextTokens, so a failed nativeLoad after a prior successful load leaves a stale value. But the only real consumer, ChatModel.kt:194, is reached exclusively through ChatScreen/MainTabs, which the top-level UI only renders while `phase is OnboardingPhase.Ready` (OnboardingScreen.kt:176). Phase only becomes/stays Ready immediately after a load() call that just succeeded (initial load, a successful model switch, or OnboardingModel's restore() on a failed switch) -- in every case the very load that produced the Ready phase also just correctly set loadedContextTokens. When load() fails and restore() also fails, phase becomes Failed and MainTabs/ChatModel unmounts, so the stale-value window exists only while the UI that would read it isn't shown. No other caller of loadedContextTokens exists in the codebase (verified via grep). The described 'any caller that reads loadedContextTokens directly without checking readiness' has no real instance in this app's architecture, so it fails the reachability lens despite being a legitimate documentation/API-contract nit.

summary: Promise.race timeout around llmService.loadModel() doesn't cancel the loser; the native load keeps running and can race a subsequent load call, leaking a native context.
failure_scenario: User selects a large model A; load exceeds timeoutMs (default 120s). doLoadTextModel's Promise.race rejects with the timeout error, ctx.onError() resets ActiveModelService.loadedTextModelId to null, ctx.onFinally() clears textLoadPromise — but the underlying llmService.loadModel(A) call (llm.ts:53-88) keeps executing natively in the background since nothing awaits or cancels it. If the user immediately retries with a different model B (a natural 'try a smaller model' UX after a timeout), loadTextModel('B') sees loadedTextModelId===null and skips the unload-before-load branch (loaders.ts:87-90); llm.ts's loadModel() guard (line 54-55) also sees this.context still null (A hasn't finished) and proceeds straight into a second concurrent initContextWithFallback() call. Whichever native init finishes last silently wins this.context; the other's LlamaContext is never released — a multi-GB native leak — and JS-side state (loadedTextModelId=B) can diverge from which model is actually resident natively.
suggested_fix: Give llmService.loadModel() its own reentrancy guard (an in-flight loadingPromise it awaits/joins, like ActiveModelService's textLoadPromise but inside llm.ts itself) so a second loadModel() call always waits for or supersedes-and-frees the first, instead of racing. At minimum, on an ActiveModelService-level timeout, keep a reference to the still-pending llmService.loadModel() promise and free/release whichever context wins once it eventually resolves, rather than abandoning it.

verdict.reason: Verified in loaders.ts and llm.ts. Promise.race only races doLoadTextModel's own await; it never cancels or awaits llmService.loadModel(A)'s underlying initContextWithFallback() call, which keeps running to completion regardless. index.ts's onFinally sets textLoadPromise=null and onError sets loadedTextModelId=null synchronously before doLoadTextModel's own promise settles, so an immediate retry with model B sees textLoadPromise===null (skips the wait-lock at index.ts:67) and loadedTextModelId===null (skips the unload branch at loaders.ts:87-90). Inside llmService.loadModel(B), the guards at llm.ts:54-55 both key off this.context, which is still null because A's initContextWithFallback() hasn't resolved yet — so B's initContextWithFallback() starts concurrently with A's. There's no locking/single-flight mechanism anywhere in llm.ts or activeModelService guarding concurrent native init, and no cancellation path exists for the loser's LlamaContext, so it is genuinely orphaned/leaked. Realistic UX (large model load exceeding the 120s default timeout, user retries with a smaller/different model) makes this reachable.

summary: executeDeleteConversationFn (and the sibling handleUnloadModelFn in useChatModelActions.ts:217) call llmService.stopGeneration() directly instead of generationService.stopGeneration(), bypassing generationService's abort bookkeeping and letting a model unload proceed without confirming the in-flight generation has actually finished natively.
failure_scenario: Mid-stream (chatStore.isStreaming=true), user deletes the active conversation. executeDeleteConversationFn (line 289-292) awaits llmService.stopGeneration() (only sends a native stop signal and flips llm.ts's own isGenerating flag) and calls chatStore.clearStreamingMessage(), but never calls generationService.stopGeneration() — contrast with handleStopFn (lines 272-275) which correctly calls both. generationService.state.isGenerating (set in generateResponse(), generationService.ts:126) stays true until the original generateResponse()'s onComplete callback eventually fires asynchronously once the native completion() promise actually settles. If the user immediately switches to another conversation and sends a message before that happens, generationService.generateResponse()/generateWithTools() hits the early-return guard at generationService.ts:115-118/198-201 ('Already generating, ignoring request') and the new message is silently dropped with no error surfaced to the user. Separately, handleUnloadModelFn (useChatModelActions.ts:214-219) does the same thing and then immediately calls activeModelService.unloadTextModel() -> llmService.unloadModel() -> context.release() (llm.ts:137-146); nothing waits for the in-flight context.completion() promise from the original send to actually resolve, so if stopCompletion() only requests a stop rather than blocking until the native decode loop unwinds, release() can free the context while a background thread is still decoding into it.
suggested_fix: Route every 'stop generation before doing X' call site through generationService.stopGeneration() (which already awaits llmService.stopGeneration() and resets abortRequested/tokenBuffer/flushTimer/isGenerating), never llmService.stopGeneration() directly. Additionally, have activeModelService.unloadTextModel() await generationService's in-flight generation settling (not just chatStore.isStreaming) before calling llmService.unloadModel(), so a free can never race an in-flight native decode.

verdict.reason: Verified in useChatGenerationActions.ts (executeDeleteConversationFn, actual lines 289-291) and useChatModelActions.ts (handleUnloadModelFn, actual lines 214-217) — both call llmService.stopGeneration() directly, unlike handleStopFn (lines 271-275) which calls both generationService.stopGeneration() and llmService.stopGeneration(). generationService.ts confirms state.isGenerating is only cleared via resetState(), which is only invoked from the onComplete callback wired into llmService.generateResponse() (generationService.ts:158-169) or from generationService.stopGeneration() itself (which forces abortRequested/resetState synchronously, generationService.ts:258-277) — neither path is triggered by a bare llmService.stopGeneration() call. The early-return guards at generationService.ts:115-118 and ~198-201 are real and confirmed, so if the original generateResponse's completion() promise hasn't yet settled by the time a new message is sent, generateResponse()/generateWithTools() returns silently without surfacing any error — a genuine, JS-level-verifiable race that doesn't depend on native library timing assumptions. The secondary claim about context.release() racing an in-flight native decode is plausible but hinges on llama.rn's stopCompletion() blocking semantics, which can't be verified from this repo alone — treated as a corroborating detail rather than the load-bearing part of the finding.

summary: Fresh-download SHA-256 verification is resolved by looking up the source URL in the curated ModelCatalog, so any model outside that static list (every sideloaded / Hugging-Face-searched GGUF) silently skips the SHA check on first download.
failure_scenario: A user searches Hugging Face (HuggingFaceModelSearch.swift) for a community GGUF and installs it. HuggingFaceCatalog.candidate(from:label:) correctly populates ModelEntry.sha256 from HF's LFS oid (HuggingFaceModelSearch.swift:176), and OnboardingModel.install() passes that ModelEntry through to the downloader and correctly re-verifies the SHA for an already-cached file (OnboardingModel.swift:199, `model.sha256`). But ModelDownloader's public protocol `download(from:to:)` takes only a URL/destination, not the ModelEntry, so ChunkedDownloadDelegate's completion handler must re-derive the expected hash: `ModelCatalog.models.first { $0.downloadURL == sourceURL }?.sha256` (line 148). `ModelCatalog.models` is the small compiled-in curated catalog — it never contains a `hf:`-search or sideloaded entry — so this lookup always returns nil for those downloads. `ModelIntegrity.verify` then falls back to a magic-header-only check (per its own gate design, matches the bug-journal's C3-2/'integrity gate downgrade' pattern), so a MITM'd or corrupted community-model download that keeps a valid GGUF header passes silently on the very download path (untrusted, community-uploaded files) where SHA verification matters most — even though the correct hash was already known and available in `model.sha256` at the OnboardingModel call site.
suggested_fix: Thread the expected SHA-256 through the download call instead of re-deriving it from a URL lookup — add an `expectedSHA256: String?` parameter to `ModelDownloader.download(from:to:)` (and `ChunkedDownloadDelegate`'s init), have `OnboardingModel.install()` pass `model.sha256` directly, and use that in place of the `ModelCatalog.models.first{...}` lookup at line 148.

verdict.reason: Confirmed by reading ModelDownloader.swift:148, OnboardingModel.swift, ModelCatalog.swift, HuggingFaceModelSearch.swift, and ModelIntegrity.swift. The public `ModelDownloader.download(from:to:)` protocol takes only a URL/destination — no ModelEntry — so `ChunkedDownloadDelegate.urlSession(_:task:didCompleteWithError:)` (line 148) resolves the expected SHA solely via `ModelCatalog.models.first { $0.downloadURL == sourceURL }?.sha256`. `ModelCatalog.models` is the small compiled-in curated list (ModelCatalog.swift). `HuggingFaceCatalog.candidate(from:label:)` builds a `ModelEntry` with `sha256: q.sha256` from HF's LFS oid and a `huggingface.co` download URL that is never in that curated array, so the lookup at line 148 returns nil for every HF-search/sideloaded install and `ModelIntegrity.verify` falls back to magic-header-only verification — even though `OnboardingModel.install()` (line 199) demonstrably already has and correctly uses `model.sha256` for the pre-existing-file re-verification path, showing the correct hash was available but simply never threaded into the fresh-download call at line 248 (`downloader.download(from: url, to: destination)` passes no sha). Both lenses pass: the code does exactly what's claimed, and community/HF-search models are a real, reachable install path.

summary: persist() unconditionally no-ops while `chat.isGenerating` is true, so switching/starting/opening a conversation mid-generation silently discards the just-sent user message (and any partial reply) with no save and no warning.
failure_scenario: User opens an existing saved conversation (savedCount = N), types a new message; ChatModel.send() appends the user turn (messages.count = N+1) and begins streaming a reply while `isGenerating == true`. Before the reply finishes, the user taps a different history item (`open(otherID)`) or 'New Chat' (`startNew()`). Both call `persist()` first (lines 63-69, 76, 85), but persist()'s guard `!chat.isGenerating` fails, so it returns without saving — `savedCount` is never advanced past N. Immediately after, `chat.restore(...)` / `chat.reset()` cancels the engine and replaces/wipes `chat.messages` (ChatModel.swift:233-244). The result: the user's just-typed message (and any tokens already streamed) is gone from both the live chat and the persisted store — there is no record of it anywhere, even though the app's own persistence invariant is 'persist on turn + switch'.
suggested_fix: Before restoring/resetting on a mid-generation switch, either (a) stop generation and persist the transcript up through the last completed message (trim the in-flight empty/partial assistant placeholder) instead of skipping the save entirely, or (b) block the switch action while `chat.isGenerating` is true and surface that in the UI (disable New Chat / history taps during generation) so the user isn't silently allowed into a data-losing action.

verdict.reason: Confirmed by reading ConversationCoordinator.swift, ChatModel.swift, and the UI call sites (ChatHomeView/ChatView in ConversationHistoryView.swift, MacRootView.swift). `persist()` (line 64) guards on `!chat.isGenerating` and returns without saving while a turn is in flight; the code's own comment even acknowledges `startNew()`/`open()` 'can run mid-stream.' Grepping all `isGenerating` usages in apple/ shows no `.disabled(chat.isGenerating)` guard on the 'New chat' toolbar button (ConversationHistoryView.swift:70) or on `onOpen`/list-row taps — only the composer's send control is disabled. So a user CAN tap 'New chat' or open another conversation mid-generation: `startNew()`/`open()` call `persist()` (no-op, isGenerating true) then immediately `chat.reset()`/`chat.restore()`, which wipes `messages` (ChatModel.swift:233-244) with no separate storage of the just-sent user turn. The onChange(of: isGenerating){!generating→persist()} handlers only fire on the ORIGINAL conversation's stream lifecycle and don't help once messages have already been replaced. Both lenses pass — this is a real, reachable, unguarded data-loss path, not merely the acknowledged 'don't save the partial assistant placeholder' tradeoff (the fully-typed user message is lost too).

summary: continueLast() has no `model` parameter and never forwards one to send(), so a Continue after a token-cap stop always resolves ChatTier.of(model: nil) (.small) for the system prompt regardless of which model/tier actually generated the original (possibly much larger) reply.
failure_scenario: A loaded 7B+ model (ChatTier.full, no length-restricting system-prompt suffix, 512-token cap) generates a long reply that hits `resolvedOptions.maxTokens`, setting `lastHitTokenCap = true`. The user taps Continue; `continueLast(options:)` (ChatModel.swift:104-107) calls `send(ChatUserFacing.continueCue(), options: options)` with no `model:` argument, so inside `send()` (line 143) `ChatTier.of(model: nil)` returns `.small`, and the system prompt gains the `.small` suffix 'Prefer 1–3 short paragraphs or a tight bullet list.' (ChatTier.swift:39) — a style constraint the original generation never had — silently changing the continuation's tone/length policy mid-conversation for a model that was never `.small`.
suggested_fix: Give `continueLast` a `model: ModelEntry? = nil` parameter and forward it to `send(_:documents:options:model:)` so the continuation uses the same tier (system prompt + token budget) as the turn it is extending.

verdict.reason: Confirmed by reading ChatModel.swift and ChatTier.swift. `continueLast(options:)` (ChatModel.swift:104-107) has no `model` parameter and calls `send(ChatUserFacing.continueCue(), options: options)` with no `model:` argument, so `send()`'s default `model: ModelEntry? = nil` applies, and `ChatTier.of(model: nil)` (ChatTier.swift:19-22) explicitly returns `.small` via its `guard let model else { return .small }`. `tier.systemPrompt` then appends the `.small` suffix ('Prefer 1-3 short paragraphs...') regardless of what tier actually produced the original reply. The UI call site in ChatView.swift:368 calls `model.continueLast()` with zero arguments, confirming this path is reachable exactly as described — a `.full`-tier (7B+) model hitting its token cap and using Continue silently picks up the `.small` system-prompt suffix. Both lenses pass: the code does what's claimed, and it's reachable via the real 'Continue' UI chip after any token-cap stop.

summary: task_done handler uses a truthy check on data.answer, so a legitimate empty-string task result is misrendered as an unexplained halt with the literal text "answered".
failure_scenario: The governed task agent (src/services/capability/capabilityAgent.ts:137) returns { answer: decision.text, steps, halt: 'answered' } where decision.text comes straight from the model's {"answer": "..."} JSON (capabilityAgent.ts:240, 'if (typeof o.answer === string) return { kind: answer, text: o.answer }' with no length/trim check). If a weak local model finishes a task with {"answer":""} after having used tools, the server sends task_done with answer: '' and halt: 'answered'. In useAgentSocket.ts the client checks 'if (data.answer)', which is false for an empty string, so it falls into the halt branch. The why lookup table (lines 268-273) has no entry for the 'answered' code, so why[data.halt] ?? data.halt evaluates to the raw string 'answered'. The UI (TasksArea.tsx) then renders a halt-styled (amber) log entry whose text is literally the word "answered" — presenting a successful completion as an unexplained failure, with no useful information for the user.
suggested_fix: Check data.answer !== null (or typeof data.answer === 'string') instead of the truthy 'if (data.answer)', and push an 'answer' log entry (with a fallback placeholder like "(no answer text)") whenever halt === 'answered', reserving the why halt-message branch for genuine non-success halts.

verdict.reason: Confirmed end-to-end: capabilityAgent.ts:240 parses {"answer":o.answer} with no length/trim check, and line 137 returns {answer: decision.text, halt:'answered'} even when decision.text is ''. websocket/index.ts:531 spreads this result verbatim into the task_done message, so answer:'' reaches the client. useAgentSocket.ts:265 does `if (data.answer)`, which is false for '', falling into the halt branch; the `why` lookup table (268-273) has no 'answered' key, so `why[data.halt] ?? data.halt` evaluates to the literal string 'answered'. No upstream guard prevents an empty-but-successful answer from taking this path.

summary: The brute-force lockout counter (failedAttempts/lockoutUntil) lives only in React component state with no persistence, so a page reload instantly resets it and lets an attacker keep guessing the privacy-lock passphrase indefinitely.
failure_scenario: PrivacyLock enforces MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS=5 then a 5-minute LOCKOUT_DURATION_MS via useState (lines 13-14), with no write to localStorage/sessionStorage anywhere in the file. A person with physical/local access to the machine (the exact threat model this lock exists for) makes 5 wrong passphrase guesses, triggering the 5-minute lockout — then simply reloads the page (F5, or reopens the app's URL). PrivacyLock remounts with failedAttempts=0 and lockoutUntil=null, so the lockout is gone and unlimited further guesses are possible immediately, defeating the entire brute-force throttle with a trivial action that requires no special access.
suggested_fix: Persist failedAttempts/lockoutUntil (e.g. under a dedicated localStorage key, separate from the plaintext-sensitive settings) and rehydrate them on mount, so a reload can't reset the attempt counter or cut a lockout short.

verdict.reason: Verified PrivacyLock.tsx declares failedAttempts/lockoutUntil via useState only (lines 13-14) with no read/write to localStorage or sessionStorage anywhere in the file, and no parent (App.tsx) tracks or persists these either. A reload remounts the component with failedAttempts=0 and lockoutUntil=null, trivially resetting the 5-attempt lockout, exactly as described. This matches the component's own stated threat model (physical/local access).

summary: The one-time plaintext-passphrase migration can clobber a passphrase the user changes while the async SHA-256 hash of the OLD passphrase is still in flight, silently reverting their new passphrase to a hash of the stale one.
failure_scenario: On mount with a legacy plaintext privacyPassphrase, the migration effect (App.tsx:412-421) sets passphraseMigratedRef.current = true and starts hashPassphrase(pp) for the OLD value. If, before that promise resolves, the user opens Settings and saves a NEW passphrase (updateSettings updates settings.privacyPassphrase and localStorage), the effect does not re-run (the ref guard short-circuits it), so the outstanding promise still resolves and calls updateSettings({ ...settingsRef.current, privacyPassphrase: h }), explicitly overwriting the just-set NEW passphrase field with h — the hash of the OLD passphrase. The user believes their new passphrase is active but the lock now expects the old one (hashed). Because hashPassphrase uses crypto.subtle.digest (sub-millisecond for a short string), the race window is extremely narrow and unlikely to be hit by normal human interaction, which keeps this at low severity/confidence.
suggested_fix: Capture the source plaintext value the hash was computed FROM, and only merge the hash in if settingsRef.current.privacyPassphrase still equals that captured plaintext (i.e. skip the merge if the user changed the passphrase in the interim).

verdict.reason: The clobber mechanism is real in the code (the .then() unconditionally overwrites privacyPassphrase with the old hash), but the reachability fails: hashPassphrase is a single crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', ...) over a short string, which resolves in well under a millisecond. The migration effect fires essentially immediately once settings load, i.e. long before a human can navigate into Settings, type a new passphrase, and click Save (a sequence that takes hundreds of milliseconds to seconds). By the time a user could ever reach the Save button, the migration promise has already resolved and settingsRef/state already reflect the hash, so the race window described is not achievable through real human interaction — the finding itself concedes this ('extremely narrow... unlikely to be hit by normal human interaction').

summary: patch_kotlin() inserts the sha256 hash right before the line's LAST ')' instead of before a trailing named `languagesLabel = "..."` argument, producing invalid Kotlin (positional arg after named arg).

summary: specs() strips positional markers (%1$@, %2$lld) down to an unordered, sorted multiset of specifier types, so the validator at line 44 accepts a translation that swaps which TYPE occupies which argument position relative to the English key.
failure_scenario: For a key with two differently-typed positional specifiers, e.g. `"Move %1$@ to folder %2$lld"` (specs = [%@, %lld]), a translation that mis-numbers the specifiers as `"...%1$lld...%2$@..."` (specifier TYPES swapped onto the other position) still normalizes via `re.sub(r'%\d+\$', '%', ...)` to the same sorted list `[%@, %lld]` as the key, so `specs(val) != ks` at line 44 is False and the mismatch is never flagged — the script's own docstring says this check exists specifically because "a mismatched %@ crashes at render." That translation ships into Localizable.xcstrings, and at runtime `String(format:)`/`String(localized:)` reads argument 1 (the actual string value) through a `%lld` specifier and argument 2 (the actual integer count) through a `%@` specifier — undefined behavior in the Objective-C/Swift varargs format path, typically a crash or garbage text on that string's render.
suggested_fix: Validate specifiers per position, not just as an unordered multiset: build an ordered map of position-number -> specifier-type for both the key and each translation (defaulting missing positional numbers to their scan order) and compare those maps directly, so a translation cannot legally reuse position N with a different specifier type than the key's position N.
